new_statements.quote: [p. 209] While in the other languages stress was predictable only in terms of phonological boundaries, in Sanɨma syntactic categories (nouns and verbs) as well as boundaries seem to be necessary. [...] Penultimate stress is still maintained in nouns when they occur without the pronoun and next to #; while a word has usually an ultimate stress because the pronoun is usually monosyllabic. [p. 211] i.e., primary stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of a nominal, pronoun and/or case morpheme; also, to the last vowel if the nominal is monosyllabic. [p. 212] For verbs and uninflected forms like interrogatives, primary stress is assigned to the last vowel if preceded by a consonant, and to the penultimate vowel if the words ends in two vowels.
new_statements.citation: Migliazza, Ernest C. 1972. Yanomama grammar and intelligibility. PhD dissertation, Indiana University. §3.61 Phonological Rules (Language D = Sanɨma/Sanumá), pp. 209-213.
new_statements.locator: pp. 209 (Primary stress placement), 211 (rule D.P.1b prose), 212 (verbs); held scanned text lines 11586-11868
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress placement is category- and morpheme-sensitive. Nominals: each nominal morpheme (noun stem, enclitic pronoun, case suffix) receives stress on its penultimate vowel (final vowel if monosyllabic); since the noun and its pronoun form one phonological word and the pronoun is usually monosyllabic, the word as a whole surfaces with final primary stress, the noun stem's stress being demoted to secondary (rule D.P.1c). A noun cited without its pronoun keeps penultimate stress. Verbs, adjectives/quantifiers not nominalised, and interrogatives: final vowel if the word ends in CV, penultimate if it ends in VV. Note: Borgman 1990:222, the catalog's Sanumá source, gives a different, length-based rule (initial in 2-3-syllable words, penultimate in longer words, secondary initial), so the two primary descriptions do not agree.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'Stress adjustment D.P.1c: primary stress is weakened by one [to secondary] when preceding another primary stress within a word' (p. 212); e.g. noun-stem stress becomes secondary before the pronoun's primary stress (examples (3)-(6), pp. 209-211).
new_statements.exceptions: Focus/emphatic speech shifts primary stress to the final vowel (D.P.1a, p. 212: 'When focusing a particular noun the stress is placed on the final vowel'); polysyllabic morphemes and sequences of two pronouns at the end of a word take penultimate stress (p. 210); presto-speech vowel loss can leave stressed final consonant-vowel sequences (pp. 212-213).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word = noun stem + enclitic pronoun/case (the citation form of a noun, 'tsai + a' house-it); stress is assigned per morpheme and adjusted at word level. The description is of Sanɨma spoken on the Auarís (Borgman's data) and Caura/Ventuari rivers; nothing in it names the Kohoroxitari village.
new_statements.identity_note: koho1245 is a Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO 639-3 code [kob] Kohoroxitari, merged into [xsu] Sanumá on 2007-07-18 (change request 2006-015: 'the name of a village of speakers of the Yanoma (or possibly the Xitari) dialect of Sanuma... a place name, rather than the name of a distinct... language variety'). Its language-level identity is therefore sanu1240 Sanumá (Yanomamic), which is ALREADY in the catalog (CATALOG_V44: rule 10 100 0010..., Borgman 1990:222, domain WORD, owner-reviewed). Ethnologue 15 (2005) had listed Kohoroxitari as 622 speakers (1976), Amazonas state, Prelazia Rio Negro, 'Unclassified. Possibly Tucanoan. May be the same as Baniwa', so the pre-merge record was itself unsure of the identity. No linguistic description of the Kohoroxitari village variety exists; the Sanumá descriptions (Borgman 1990, Autuori 2013/2019: Auaris, Roraima; Migliazza 1972: Auaris/Caura/Ventuari) do not name it. Under the census law (retired codes confer no identity) this entry should not become a separate catalog record.

sources.note: First-hand rules for Sanɨma (= Sanumá): stress depends on syntactic category; nominals (noun + enclitic pronoun/case forming one phonological word) get primary stress on the penultimate vowel of each nominal morpheme, last vowel if monosyllabic, then a stress-adjustment rule demotes all but the last primary stress to secondary; verbs and uninflected forms get final stress after a consonant, penultimate if the word ends in two vowels; focus/emphasis shifts stress to the final vowel (pp. 209-213). Data from the Auaris/Caura/Ventuari Sanɨma, not from a Kohoroxitari village.
